en: Acceptance act: the record of stores and herd taken over after the second harvest. Actual stocks are recorded; earlier losses are never audited. Guardable stores are audited from acceptance. The chairman answers for yearly herd deaths from feed shortage from the year after.
Audit: a check of store records. After the acceptance act, losses are checked where a guard can be posted. Church and storage-clamp losses are excluded.

Auditor's warning: issued for a shortage of 5% or more. At 10% or more, a trial is possible only after a warning at the previous audit and no sooner than 15 months after acceptance, from the start of year four.
Off-book funds: income kept out of the accounts. A check may uncover what was hidden.
Cart: a wagon harnessed to a horse for transport. It carries cargo and can give people a lift.
Rotation step: one year in a field's crop sequence. If winter crops are not sown within their window, the field stays fallow that year.
Civil registry: the office that officially records births, marriages and other events in a person's life.
Storage clamp: potatoes or root crops piled by a field and covered with straw and earth. No guard can be posted at a clamp. Its losses are not audited; the food can be moved to guarded storage.
Tally clerk: the person who draws up work assignments, assigns people to jobs and takes their skills into account.
Crop rotation: a field's crop sequence across the years. The chairman sets it in advance; field work follows this sequence.
Discount: a reduction in what must be paid or returned. With a good reputation, the district may reduce a loan's markup.
Draft animals: working animals that pull carts and farm implements. On the kolkhoz, horses do this work.
Fallow: a field worked this year but not sown with an ordinary crop. Winter rye can be sown there in late summer for next year's harvest.
Abandoned land: land once plowed but left unworked for years and now overgrown. It can be brought back into use as a field.
Feed shortage: not enough food for animals. Underfed livestock cope less well with cold and disease.
Feed unit: a measure of nutritional value, not weight. One unit equals the nutrition in a kilogram of oats. Equal weights of different feeds need not provide equal nutrition.
Rural medical post: a small village clinic providing first aid and maternity care. More complex cases require a hospital.
Floodplain: low ground beside a river that may flood when the water rises. In the game, it cannot be built on, but its meadows can be used.
Feed balance: comparing feed stocks with what livestock need until the next supply arrives.
Fuels and lubricants: fuel runs the engine; lubricants reduce friction and wear in machinery parts.
Reserve: stocks set aside for seed, feed or another farm need. Releasing a reserve permits its use now; there may not be enough left for its original purpose.
Goods loan: food or feed borrowed from the district. It is repaid in the same goods, with a markup, in addition to the plan.
Harness: straps and fittings connecting a horse to a cart or implement. The horse cannot do that work without a serviceable harness.
Harrowing: working the soil with a harrow after plowing. It breaks up clods and levels the surface before sowing.
Haymaking: mowing, drying and gathering grass for livestock feed. Rain during drying hinders this work.
Household plot: a family's own garden and animals. Its produce belongs to the family, not the kolkhoz.
Distribution rate: how much produce is due for earned labor-day credits. More than the available stocks cannot be issued.
Labor-day credit: a measure of work done, used to distribute produce to families from storage. Difficult or skilled work earns more credits. It is not a calendar day or money.
Allocation: points used to obtain scarce goods and machinery from the district. They are not money; unused points expire at year-end.
Livestock mortality: animals dying from disease, age or other causes. It is a loss of animals, not a sale or planned slaughter.
Loan markup: an addition to what was borrowed. With a good reputation, the district may reduce this addition.
Logging plot: an area set aside for timber harvesting. In the game, logging outside the forest is marked with the Stake logging plot order.
Low water: the period when the river is low. In bridge repair arrangements, it means the time after the water falls.
Milk yield: the quantity of milk obtained from a cow or herd over a stated period.
Machine and tractor station (MTS): the district sends machinery and a crew on request for allocation points.

Night pasture: summer grazing for horses at night. In the game, schoolchildren watch them during the holidays; the herd returns to the stable in the morning. Available after a horse yard is established.
Offspring: young animals born to the herd, such as calves and foals. They are counted separately from adult livestock.
Own draft power: the share of all work in the last completed year done with kolkhoz horses. Manual work and the district's visiting machinery crew do not increase this share.
Party cell: a local group of party members on the kolkhoz. They meet to discuss shared affairs. A local party organizer arranges the group's work.
Person-day: one person's work for a working day, a measure of labor used. A labor-day credit is an entitlement used to distribute produce to a family.
Plan item: a line stating how much of one product must be delivered to the district. Delivering another product does not replace it.
Quarry: an open site for extracting stone, staked where suitable rock is available.
District land office: the department that sends the kolkhoz its produce delivery plan.
Ration: an allotted portion of food or feed. If a family is underfed, the chairman issues a minimum ration from storage regardless of labor-day credits, reducing stocks for other needs.
Reputation: the district's assessment of the farm. Meeting the plan raises it; failing lowers it. Being under scrutiny means being in bad standing.
All-hands rush: an order to speed up one job, such as a field's harvest. People work harder, tire faster and are less satisfied. The rush can be canceled at any time.
Satisfaction: how well a family lives on the kolkhoz. It depends on food, housing, rest and other living conditions, and affects family members' work. Mood is an individual resident's personal state.
Seed reserve: grain and potatoes kept for the next sowing. Only the chairman can release it for food. What is eaten now cannot be sown for the next harvest.
Seed loan: seeds borrowed from the district. By the turn of the year, the same product is returned with a markup, in addition to the plan.
Underground entrepreneur: someone who runs production and trade outside the accounts.
Underground entrepreneur: someone who runs production and trade outside the accounts. The Dealer is good at making arrangements and is especially strong in this business.
Shoal: shallow water near the bank. Construction sand is taken from a suitable staked site.
Shortage: an unrecorded loss of produce. Audits calculate it per product: losses over the last 24 months divided by receipts over that period. Products with less than 2 t received are not checked.
Silage: moist feed made from chopped plants preserved without air. In the game, it is stored in a silage trench or tower and fed to cows.
Breeding male: an adult male used to produce young. Without one, the herd will have no new offspring.
Komsomol placement: the youth league refers a young specialist to work on a kolkhoz. The chairman requests the required profession from the district.
Spring crops: crops sown in spring and harvested in the same year.
Standing assignment: an assignment that stays until canceled; the work repeats under a set condition. No need to issue a new one each time.
Livestock boarding: temporarily keeping kolkhoz animals in household yards while collective livestock sheds lack space.
Stubble: short stalks left in a field after grain harvest. It is not a new sowing, but the remains of the harvested crop.
Threshing: separating grain from the ears after reaping. The grain and straw then go their separate ways.
Draft power: a horse's ability to pull a plow or harrow. Draft animals are the animals themselves. On hay alone, horses plow and harrow less effectively.
Turn of the year: New Year begins. The district totals produce deliveries, debts are recalculated and a new annual plan starts.
Building level: one of a building's successive stages. The first comes with construction; the next adds space, equipment or a new job in the same building.
Autumn plowing: preparing a field for spring sowing. After harvest and hauling, workers plow under the tally clerk's or chairman's assignment. Only harrowing and sowing remain in spring.
